Regarding what Rabbainu said: "Mein zach vet zeyn nisht oisluzin — nitzachti v'anatzayach" [My thing will not be abandoned — I have prevailed and I shall prevail] — which is the aspect of netzach [eternity/victory] — I heard from my friend Reb Mordechai the ritual slaughterer of blessed memory that the following is hinted at in Tehillim, at the end of Psalm 16, where the verse concludes: "pleasantness at Your right hand, netzach" [Tehillim 16:11] — these three words in the Mesorah appear three times, for they hint at three Tzaddikim who are explicitly described as being in the aspect of netzach: King Dovid, Mordechai the righteous, and our holy master Rabbainu.

Ne'imos [pleasantness] — this hints at King Dovid, of whom it is written "the sweet singer of Yisrael" [Shmuel II 23:1], and we always say "Dovid, King of Yisrael, lives and endures" — which is the aspect of netzach. Biminecha [at Your right hand] — this hints at Mordechai the righteous, who is ben Yemini [of the tribe of Binyamin / son of the right], and of him it is written "their memory shall not depart from their descendants" [Esther 9:28] — which is also the aspect of netzach. And finally the verse concludes with netzach — which hints at our holy master Rabbainu, who said explicitly about himself: "Mein zach vet zeyn nisht oisluzin" — which is the aspect of netzach. And his holy name in gematria [numerology] equals netzach, and his sefirah is netzach. And therefore his passing was on the fourth day of Sukkos, which is the day of Moshe Rabbainu whose sefirah is netzach — as is known.

It follows that these three words hint at the three Tzaddikim who are in the aspect of netzach — with good reason and understanding. And through this I can also explain what is written of Mordechai: "And Mordechai walked before the court of the women's house" [Esther 2:11] — which Rabbainu explained in Likutay Moharan 56: that the verse explains how the true Tzaddik rectifies the three lower spiritual levels that are distant from Hashem, called in the aspect of women. That is: some are in the aspect of those who have fled and jumped from their place in the world — having distanced themselves from Hashem; some were once somewhat close to Hashem but have already forgotten Him — called nashim from the language of forgetting, as in "for G-d has made me forget" [Bereishis 41:51]; and some still remember Hashem but their strength has weakened and they have no power to overpower their inclination. All three of these lower levels are rectified by Mordechai — who is the aspect of the true Tzaddik — for by walking before them always, as a guide who walks before people to show them the way, he shows them the path on which to walk and return to Hashem. Until in the end he rectifies all of them, even those who have fallen so low in the three levels described.

And we find this also with our holy and awesome master Rabbainu — who said explicitly: "Vus hot ir moireh tzu hub'n — az ich gei far aich" [What do you have to fear? — for I walk before you!] For our holy and awesome master Rabbainu, who is the true Tzaddik unto the end of all generations, warned and promised us that he walks before us — even before lowly ones like us in these generations — and he always walks before us to show us the path in which to go, and smooths the path before us of all kinds of pits and thorns and snakes and scorpions. For as his power was then in his holy lifetime, so is his power now — and certainly his power and holy merit are even greater and greater now. For the Tzaddikim are greater in their death than in their lifetimes. Therefore we have nothing to fear and nothing to be frightened of or fallen by from anything in the world — neither in material matters nor in spiritual matters — only to strengthen and fortify ourselves in the power and merit of our holy and awesome master Rabbainu. And through him we have good hope that we will merit a good end and eternal life, Amen.

I heard from our dear friend, the veteran Chassid famous among the followers — his name was Reb Moshe of Breslov, of blessed and righteous memory — who grew up in Reb Noson's home from his childhood and served him there, as is known to the followers. He told me that once when Reb Noson traveled to Uman for Erev Rosh Chodesh to Rabbainu's holy grave, he took Reb Moshe along to serve him on the journey. Reb Noson's practice was to hire a wagon with the driver in such a way that the wagon he traveled in would be covered like an enclosed room — so that he could pray and learn there and fulfill "you shall speak in them" — "and when you walk on the road" [Devarim 6:7].

When evening came they stopped at an inn to rest for the night, and then traveled several hours before dawn. When dawn broke, Reb Noson put on his tallis and covered his holy face with it as was always his way during prayer, and began to recite the order of prayer — the blessings and the sacrificial passages and the incense — in a low voice and very broken heart — quite unlike his usual manner. He then began to recite Hodu too in a low voice and broken heart, and Reb Moshe found it wondrous — for Reb Noson's practice was always to pray with joy and fervor and with calling out, and now he was praying without any fervor, only in a low voice and a broken heart like someone who yearns and longs and entreats to attain something. The bitterness that Reb Noson had was so great that Reb Moshe too was moved and his heart broke within him to pieces literally, and he began to weep tears continuously without pause.

When Reb Noson reached the psalm "A Song of the dedication of the house" [Tehillim 30] and the verse "Sing to Hashem, His devout ones" [30:5] — he stopped and was silent for several moments without any word. Reb Moshe did not know what this was about. Then Reb Noson began to sing the melody of Eishes Chayil in a very awesome voice and great deveykus [cleaving] — without words, only the melody itself — until Reb Moshe could not sit in the wagon from fear, and literally his whole body was trembling and his knees knocking together from the overwhelming fear that fell upon him then. Reb Noson sang thus for about twenty minutes. Suddenly Reb Noson clapped his hands many times — literally splitting the heavens — and began to cry out "Sing to Hashem, His devout ones, and give thanks to His holy memory" [Tehillim 30:5] in powerful voices and great joy. And so he prayed the rest of the prayer with clapping and awesome voices and a wondrous deveykus that is impossible to imagine in any way.

During this they came to a village at early morning. The shepherds there were driving the cattle to the fields to graze, and the villagers each went to their work. When they heard such voices and clapping from within the wagon, they were startled and astonished — for they had never heard such wondrous voices. The wagon traveled swiftly on its way. The shepherds began running after the wagon, and all the village people — young and old — ran after the wagon in excitement for a great distance from the village — to hear the deveykus and the pleasantness of Reb Noson's voice. Reb Moshe told me that the overwhelming beauty and magnificence of this sight was wondrous and awesome — for they saw with their own eyes how all the world and its fullness — the crops and the grasses and the trees and the animals and people — all raced and yearned to be included in Reb Noson's prayer. This was literally as is written in Rabbainu's words in Likutay Moharan Part II, section 1 — Tik'u: "For this is the obligation of all the grasses and all the vegetation of the field — when a person stands to pray, since he is in the aspect of the word of Hashem which is their supernal root, they return their strength into the prayer which is their supernal root." And then Reb Moshe saw this fulfilled in practice with Reb Noson.

Until in the end everyone was compelled to turn back — to their work and to graze their cattle. Reb Noson knew nothing of all this because of his tremendous fervor in prayer. When Reb Noson reached "The support of our fathers" in the prayer they came to another village, and the driver wanted to rest a bit and feed the horses. There was a Jewish inn there and the driver turned to enter. Reb Moshe did not know what to do — how to disturb Reb Noson now in the middle of such fervor before the Shemoneh Esrei. But when the wagon went to enter the gate of the inn, the wheels struck the threshold — which was a very large and thick beam — and when they went over it, the wheels hit the ground with such force that Reb Noson felt the strong impact and was silent for a moment and understood they had come to some inhabited place. Then Reb Moshe could approach him and took him by the hand and led him into the inn — though Reb Noson was still crying out "and He answers His people Yisrael" in powerful voices, covered in his tallis. They stood him by one wall of the inn.

When Reb Noson finished the prayer and removed the Rashi tefillin and wanted to put on the Rabbenu Tam tefillin, he said to Reb Moshe: "Certainly you wonder at what happened at the beginning of my prayer — why I was with such a broken heart — and what made me pause at the psalm of dedication — and why I began to sing the melody of Eishes Chayil. What shall I tell you, my beloved student? I put it in my heart at the beginning of the prayer — where I am traveling, to Uman for Erev Rosh Chodesh for Rabbainu's holy grave. And I remembered that my practice in Rabbainu's lifetime when I came before him was that he would ask me: 'What is new with you? Do you have any renewal in your service from our conversations of before?' And so on. Now when I come to Rabbainu's grave and I do not feel such a renewal within myself — my heart broke within me and I began to pray with a broken heart and great shame — with bowed face: 'how shall I enter before his holy grave?' — until almost no life force remained in me. I did not know with what to revive myself. Hashem helped me with His great mercy and kindness — I remembered what Rabbainu had said to me: 'Ven men hot zech shoyn gor nisht mit vus m'chieh tzu zayn, iz men zech mchieh mit a nigun' [When one has absolutely nothing with which to revive oneself, one revives oneself with a melody]. I began to think: with which melody to revive myself? And I remembered the overwhelming life force I had when I heard the first melody from Rabbainu on the first Shabbos of my attachment to him — which is this melody of Eishes Chayil. Joy entered my heart immensely and I strengthened myself greatly, and the melody was renewed for me enormously — and I began to sing it anew with the wondrous life force of that very life force I had then on the first Shabbos with Rabbainu. About this it says: 'You shall come, you shall gaze from the top of Amana' [Shir HaShirim 4:8] — 'from the top' specifically — meaning the melody I heard at the head and beginning of my attachment to him. And through this I revived myself greatly. Then I reflected: now I must say the verse 'Sing to Hashem, His devout ones' — and thank G-d I am of his devout ones, and even now I travel to his holy grave for Erev Rosh Chodesh. I said to my heart: 'It is good to give thanks to Hashem and to praise His great Name for all the kindness and goodness He has done with me' — and from all this I strengthened myself and began to pray with a new mind and new life force — and this is 'give thanks to His holy memory.'"

Reb Moshe's eyes shed many tears as he recounted this — from the great emotion he had felt at the time of telling it, remembering all that had happened on that journey — which is impossible to explain or recount orally, certainly not in writing. He said that from then his heart opened and he began to understand a little of how it is possible to live such a wondrous life in prayer — through the power of our holy master Rabbainu. He had not known this before — had not seen such a wonder — how from such bitterness as Reb Noson had beforehand, there came afterward such enormous joy in fervor and holy awe — so wondrous and astounding.
